name: csv-zero (Zig SIMD CSV field iterator)
baseline: CSV parser labelled 'zsc (c)' in the csv-race results (the csv-race README text calls the C SIMD parser zsv, and its Makefile builds src/c/zsv with `cc -O3 main.c -lzsv`) and lazycsv (C++); the same table also measures Rust simd-csv and csv.
workload: csv-race: iterate a whole CSV file, count the fields, 64 KB input buffer where configurable; four real-world files (nfl.csv, worldcitiespop.csv, MBTA stop times, game.csv) and generated files from about 1 KB to about 9.9 GB; wall time plus perf counters.
claimed_speedup: csv-race README: 'csv-zero finishes first across all tested cases' on the large files; csv-zero README: 'this library comes on top'. From result-all.csv, wall time csv-zero vs zsc (C) vs lazycsv (C++): ~9.9 GB mixed-quote 12-column file 7.73 s vs 12.7 s vs 12.1 s; ~3.2 GB no-quote 52-column file 603 ms vs 1.32 s vs 1.65 s; ~696 MB 2-column many-rows file 574 ms vs 1.50 s vs 1.25 s; nfl.csv 775 us vs 1.78 ms vs 2.12 ms; game.csv 2.86 ms vs 6.71 ms vs 3.10 ms. Ratios (derived from page data): 1.6x over both on the 9.9 GB file, 2.2x over zsc and 2.7x over lazycsv on the 3.2 GB file, 2.6x and 2.2x on the 696 MB file; only 1.08x over lazycsv on game.csv.
compiler_and_flags: Zig: `zig build --release=fast` (csv-race README lists Zig 0.15.2); C: `cc -O3 main.c -lzsv` (compiler not named; the 'zsc (c)' binary is a manual build whose flags are not in the repo); C++: `g++ -std=c++17 -O3 -march=native`; Rust: `cargo build --release`.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5 PRO 5650U, 30 GB RAM, Linux 6.17.8-arch1-1 (csv-race README)
why_faster: csv-zero README: zero-allocation, field-by-field iterator (no record abstraction), SIMD-accelerated scanning with a tunable vector length; the author's blog post with the details was not opened.
stars_or_usage: 38 stars; the Zig CSV parser used by the LangArena Zig CSV::Parse entry
tradeoffs: Deliberately minimal: iterates fields only (no records, no type conversion, no allocation unless the caller copies), strict RFC 4180 and rejects malformed input. The C API is slower than the Zig API (README says it still beats every parser in csv-race).
caveats: Author-run benchmark in the author's own companion repo, on a low-power laptop CPU. The task only counts fields, so conversion and copying costs are not measured. The committed result-all.csv lists only the top five parsers per case (csv-parser, rapidcsv, the Go parser and csv_core rows are not in it). The C parser build is manual and its flags are not in the repo; the 'zsc' versus 'zsv' naming is inconsistent between the README text and the charts. Not the clear winner on every file (lazycsv is within 8% on game.csv, and Rust simd-csv is 1.44x behind on the 3.2 GB file, derived).
found_via: Followed from the LangArena Zig dependency list (zig/build.zig.zon, csvzero) to the csv-zero README and the csv-race repo; no search query surfaced it.

name: z-fasta (Zig FASTA index, extract and stats tool)
baseline: samtools faidx 1.24 with HTSlib 1.24 (C); also measured: fastahack, SeqKit (Go), noodles and rust-bio (Rust), pyfaidx (Python).
workload: Build a samtools-compatible .fai index (`z-fasta index --emit-fai`) of uncompressed FASTA (human genome ~2.9 GiB, transcriptome ~459 MiB, proteome ~13 MiB), and fetch one 1 kbp region through an existing index; warm cache.
claimed_speedup: README (v0.3.5, measured 2026-10-10): .fai index build, z-fasta vs samtools: human genome 0.3824 s vs 8.1614 s (21.3x in the index report's speedup table), transcriptome 0.1546 s vs 1.7112 s (11.1x), proteome 0.0113 s vs 0.0650 s (about 5.8x, derived from page data); fastahack 20.8901 s on the genome (54.6x). One 1 kbp GET: human genome 2.3 ms vs 8.2 ms, transcriptome 8.2 ms (.zfi) vs 301.8 ms, proteome 2.7 ms vs 17.9 ms.
compiler_and_flags: z-fasta 0.3.5 built with Zig 0.16.0, `zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dstrip=true`; samtools 1.24 and HTSlib 1.24 built from source by tools/install.sh with plain `./configure` and `make` (no custom CFLAGS in the lines read, so package defaults apply; compiler not named).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X (README); zebrac 0.6.2 runner, 5 measured samples after 3 warmups, warm cache
tradeoffs: Uncompressed FASTA only; own .zfi index plus samtools-compatible .fai for representable FASTA; one static executable (about 800 KiB) with no runtime dependencies; scope limited to index, get, validate and stats.
caveats: First-party benchmark with the author's own runner and reports; no mechanism is stated in the README parts read, and thread use by either tool is not stated. The 7.9 GB/s indexing throughput on the genome points to page-cache-bound warm runs. The rust-bio lane is a custom FAI writer, not a rust-bio command, and the stats table compares against SeqKit, not samtools. samtools was built with default flags rather than -O3 -march=native.
found_via: GitHub topic page https://github.com/topics/simd?l=zig (listed as 'z-fasta, 9 stars').

name: cuniq (Rust unique-line counter)
baseline: GNU coreutils 8.32 `sort -u | wc -l` and `sort | uniq -c`, and GNU awk 5.3.2 (`a[$0]++`), all C programs.
workload: Count distinct lines (and per-line occurrence counts) of a 32 GiB preprocessed Wikipedia text dump with 6,028,206,370 lines, 78,035,032 of them unique; also a 4,000,000-line random-number file in criterion benches.
claimed_speedup: PERFORMANCE.md, 32 GiB test: `sort -u huge.txt | wc -l` 14m11.935s vs `cuniq --memmap --threads=1` 2m47.462s (5.1x, derived from page data), `cuniq --memmap --mode=near-exact` (16 threads) 59.387 s (14.3x, derived), `--mode=estimate` (HyperLogLog, 0.74% error) 9.038 s. Report mode: `sort | uniq -c` 28m46.811s and awk 25m03.082s vs `cuniq --memmap -c` 3m07.817s (9.2x and 8.0x, derived). README: 'For counting cuniq reliably outperforms GNU sort in all cases', with one exception for reports on inputs with almost no duplicates.
compiler_and_flags: Rust nightly with `RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native" cargo +nightly build -Z build-std=std --target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` (recipe in PERFORMANCE.md, with profile-guided optimization mentioned); GNU tools are prebuilt Windows binaries run from Git Bash, build flags unknown.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D (16 threads), 5200 MT/s memory, 6950 MB/s sequential disk read, Windows 11 24H2
why_faster: PERFORMANCE.md optimization list: hash table instead of sorting (O(n)), memory-mapped input, memchr newline search, no UTF-8 validation, ahash, leaking large structures instead of freeing, multithreaded hashing and HyperLogLog for the estimate mode.
stars_or_usage: crates.io and AUR packages (per README); star count not seen
tradeoffs: Exact mode keeps every distinct line in memory; near-exact mode ignores 64-bit hash collisions; estimate mode is approximate; -c output is unsorted unless -s; hashing loses to sorting when nearly every line is unique.
caveats: First-party and Windows-only harness: the GNU baseline is coreutils 8.32 and gawk 5.3.2 under Git Bash, which may be a weaker baseline than a Linux build (sort thread count and flags unknown). The win is an algorithm change (hash versus sort), not a language effect. The author's own table also measures huniq 2.7.0 (6m04.595s count), runiq and sortuniq. GPL licence.
found_via: WebSearch: "faster than GNU" wc OR sort OR uniq OR cut OR sed OR awk written in Rust OR Zig OR Go OR Nim benchmark github README

name: huniq (Rust sort-free uniq)
baseline: `sort | uniq` / `sort -u` and `sort | uniq -c` with GNU sort and GNU uniq (C), awk, GNU datamash (C), and the author's earlier C++ implementation huniq version 1.
workload: Remove duplicate lines (and count occurrences with -c) from data built by repeating /usr/share/dict word lists 1 to 100 times (benchmark.sh).
claimed_speedup: readme.md table (seconds / peak KB): uniq mode, 1 repetition: huniq2-rust 0.26 s vs huniq1-c++ 1.67 s, awk 1.63 s, datamash 1.78 s, `sort | uniq` 7.30 s; 100 repetitions: 43.65 s vs 154.99 s (C++), 239.66 s (awk), 285.94 s (datamash), 1062.07 s (sort | uniq). Count mode, 100 repetitions: 90.80 s vs 150.41 s (C++), 163.13 s (awk), 322.70 s (datamash), 933.67 s (sort | uniq). README: 'beats the C++ implementation by a factor of between 6.5 ... and 3.5', 'compared to sort -u: huniq is around 30 times faster', 'between 5x and 10x faster than sort | uniq -c'. Memory: about 29.5 MB vs 26.2 MB (C++) in uniq mode, 132 MB vs 60 MB in count mode.
compiler_and_flags: `cargo build --release` (Cargo.toml: edition 2018, ahash, bstr, clap); C++ version 1 build flags not stated.
why_faster: README: 'Sorting is slow. By using hash tables/hash sets instead of sorting the input'. Why the Rust rewrite beats the author's C++ version 1 is not explained.
tradeoffs: Single-threaded; holds all distinct lines in memory (README: use datamash for memory efficiency); -c output order is not stable.
caveats: Author-run with no machine, compiler or tool versions stated; benchmark.sh loops until aborted. Inputs are dictionary files repeated N times. The C++ comparator is the author's own earlier tool, so the 3.5x to 6.5x says little about Rust versus C++ in general. Hash versus sort is an algorithm difference. A competitor's table (cuniq PERFORMANCE.md) measured huniq 2.7.0 at 6m04.595s on a 32 GiB file against 14m11.935s for `sort -u | wc -l`.

name: wz (Rust wc replacement)
baseline: GNU wc (C); version and locale not stated (GitHub Actions runner).
workload: hyperfine (100 runs, 2 warmups) of wz against wc for `-c` bytes, `-w` words, `-m` chars, `-l` lines, `-L` max line length, default mode, and a high-load case (the file list tripled), over a folder of files that BENCH.md does not describe.
claimed_speedup: BENCH.md means (wz vs wc): chars 1.9 ms vs 19.8 ms (10.5x); default mode 7.3 ms vs 21.4 ms (2.95x); words 7.5 ms vs 20.5 ms (2.72x); high load 14.9 ms vs 58.2 ms (3.9x); lines 1.8 ms vs 2.2 ms (1.2x). Bytes is the other way: wz 1.9 ms vs wc 0.8 ms (wz 2.44x slower).
compiler_and_flags: Cargo.toml release profile: opt-level 2, fat LTO, codegen-units 1, panic abort, strip; GNU wc build not stated.
hardware: GitHub Actions runner, Intel Xeon Platinum 8272CL @ 2.60 GHz, 2 vCPUs (BENCH.md)
why_faster: README only says 'heavily optimized for performance' and uses rayon to count several files in parallel.
tradeoffs: UTF-8 aware counting with table or JSON output; UTF-16 support listed as coming later; parallel over multiple files.
caveats: Input files and sizes are not described (runs of 2 to 20 ms suggest small inputs where process start-up matters). The char and word wins probably reflect glibc wc's multibyte path in a UTF-8 locale rather than raw scan speed (inference, locale unstated). wz loses the plain byte count. The GNU wc version is the runner's distribution binary. No commits since 2023-08.
found_via: GitHub topic page https://github.com/topics/utf-8?l=rust (description 'Faster alternative to GNU wc with UTF-8 support').

name: zigmark (Zig CommonMark parser and renderer)
baseline: cmark and cmark-gfm (C); the same table also lists lowdown and discount (C) and pandoc (Haskell).
workload: Convert the repository's own 27 KB README.md from Markdown to HTML on the command line; hyperfine mean wall time per process, plus peak RSS (`nix run .#bench`).
claimed_speedup: README table (updated 2026-06-04), mean ms: lowdown 2.2, zigmark ReleaseFast 2.4, discount 2.7, zigmark ReleaseSmall 2.9, zigmark ReleaseSafe 4.4, cmark 5.3, cmark-gfm 5.6, pandoc 185.4. So zigmark ReleaseFast is about 2.2x faster than cmark and 2.3x faster than cmark-gfm (derived from page data), ReleaseSafe about 1.2x; lowdown is faster than zigmark. Peak RSS: zigmark ReleaseSmall 1952 KB, ReleaseFast 2412 KB vs cmark 4336 KB and cmark-gfm 4300 KB.
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0, ReleaseFast / ReleaseSmall / ReleaseSafe builds; cmark build flags and version not stated.
tradeoffs: Two-pass parser built on the mecha parser-combinator library; passes the CommonMark spec tests (652) and 24 GFM extension tests per README; also offers Typst and Markdown renderers, frontmatter handling and a C ABI. Noncommercial licence (not OSI-approved).
caveats: One 27 KB input, so the 2 to 5 ms process times are dominated by start-up and file I/O; no CPU or machine stated; baseline cmark flags unknown; benchmark output is auto-written into the README by the repo's own bench app. lowdown (C) beats it. The licence forbids commercial use, so the code is reference-only.

name: The Platinum Searcher (pt, Go code search)
baseline: The Silver Searcher (ag, written in C) and ack (Perl).
workload: Recursive search for EXPORT_SYMBOL_GPL in the Linux kernel source tree, timed with the shell `time` builtin (one run per tool).
claimed_speedup: README benchmark: ack 32.613 s total (99% cpu), ag 1.069 s total (1.57s user 1.76s system, 311% cpu), pt 0.991 s total (2.29s user 1.26s system, 358% cpu). README claims pt searches 'as fast as' ag and 3 to 5x faster than ack. pt is about 8% faster than ag by wall time (derived from page data) but uses more CPU time (3.55 s vs 3.33 s, derived).
tradeoffs: Honours .gitignore, skips dot-directories unless --hidden, reads UTF-8, EUC-JP and Shift_JIS; binaries for macOS, Windows and Linux (README).
caveats: Single run on an unspecified machine, with no tool versions or flags, from the Travis CI era; an 8% wall-time gap is within the noise of one run. ripgrep (already in the catalog) is the more common choice today. ag is described as C only by inference from its README (it asks 'Do you know C?').
found_via: Recalled as a Go grep alternative while reviewing GitHub grep topic pages; its README was opened directly (no search query surfaced it).

name: Zig (benchLANG strings workload, 19x19 word equality)
baseline: C (GCC 16.2.0, `-O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops`, glibc memcmp per equal-length pair) and C++ (g++ same flags, std::string_view ==, libstdc++).
workload: benchLANG 'Strings': 5M iterations of comparing every pair of the 19 words of a constant sentence for equality (19x19 pairs per iteration).
claimed_speedup: README results table (Sept 2026, one run per language), Strings column: Zig 1.504 s, C 2.132 s, C++ 2.190 s, Go 2.532 s, Rust 2.621 s, Nim 2.804 s. Zig is 1.42x faster than C and 1.46x faster than C++ (derived from page data). Zig is not faster overall: on the Fibonacci workload Zig is 3.181 s vs C 1.694 s, and C ranks first on total runtime (9.762 s vs Zig 10.737 s).
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0 `zig build-exe -OReleaseFast -mcpu=native -fstrip -lc`; C `gcc -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off -s` and C++ `g++ -std=c++20` with the same flags, GCC 16.2.0 from nixpkgs-unstable.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X locked at 3.5 GHz, 48 GB DDR4-3600, Arch Linux; one run per language, 3 September 2026
tradeoffs: ReleaseFast removes Zig's safety checks. The Nix flake pins every toolchain, and the analyzer marks the ranking invalid if checksums differ between languages (README).
caveats: The source states no mechanism, so this is capped at C. Reading the code (my inference, not the source's): both versions compare lengths first and then bytes; C calls memcmp for each equal-length pair while Zig's std.mem.eql is inlined, so the gap may be call overhead on tiny strings. The input is a 19-word compile-time constant (README warns constants can be folded), a single run per language, and Rust and Go are slower than C on the same task. The same repository ranks C first overall.
